title: Ottawa man 'defiant' in deadly standoff with Toronto police
article: Julie Knetsch tried desperately to pry an air gun from Devon LaFleur's hands seconds before Toronto police opened fire, killing the 30-year-old Ottawa man who had a history of mental illness.

The circumstances of his death are now the subject of a Special Investigations Unit probe, after a dozen Toronto police surrounded the couple outside a North York women's shelter Friday night, with three officers firing at a "defiant" LaFleur.
For Knetsch, it was "a completely inconceivable" outcome to a drama that unfolded throughout that day.

Knetsch and LaFleur were former lovers who reunited in February after a split 12 years ago.
Last week, LaFleur contacted her, saying his phone had been stolen and asking for her number and address in Toronto, where she had been staying at a shelter near Bayview Avenue and Steeles.
Then, on Friday afternoon, Knetsch got a call from LaFleur's sister, Sascha.

"She said her car was missing and her father's air gun was missing, and Devon was missing. They had reason to believe he was coming to see me," Knetsch told the Citizen, recounting the events that led to the deadly confrontation.
Knetsch also learned that police were looking for LaFleur in connection with a gunpoint bank robbery in Kanata earlier that day.
He had been in trouble with the law before, once in connection with a 2007 bank robbery at age 21, and again after a 2009 armed robbery at a Bank Street video store.
"By that time it was well-known that he was on the run and had robbed a bank and was looking for me, so the police got ahold of me" said Knetsch, who said she was not at all fearful.

Around the same time, Ottawa police posted a bulletin warning of a missing man who may have been armed with a handgun. Knetsch insists the police officers she spoke with were fully aware that he was carrying an air gun. LaFleur's aunt, Janet Andersen, told reporters "he was not a dangerous man," and said his family informed police of the missing air gun when they reported him missing Friday.
Toronto police, Ottawa police and the SIU have declined to comment.

"I had spoken with his dad, Malcolm, and we agreed that if I was there, it would get defused and he would go peaceably. If I had any premonition this would happen..." Knetsch said, her voice trailing off.
Knetsch kept getting calls from random numbers throughout the evening. LaFleur was stopping along the way and paying strangers for the use of their cell phones.
They arranged a rendezvous at the Centerpoint Mall in North York. She relayed the information to police, who said they would be waiting for them at a Tim Hortons inside the shopping centre.
But LaFleur arrived late. He had ditched the car after apparently getting lost in the city, with no phone, no familiarity with Toronto and, according to Knetsch, "a lot of money on him."
Around 9 p.m., LaFleur pulled up to the mall in a city cab.
"So we embraced and he was really happy," Knetsch recalled, "But he was very hyper."
She learned LaFleur, who suffered from bipolar disorder, had been off his medication for several days.
He excitedly described the morning bank robbery as if it was a scene from a movie.
"He was telling me how he was so charming (in the bank). He was like, 'Sorry ladies I didn't mean to upset you,' and kind of bowed (to the tellers) and was graceful when he left the bank."
Knetsch led LaFleur to the coffee shop, but by that time, the mall had closed.
The couple hopped in a cab, and from the back seat, Knetsch texted police the address of their destination: the women's shelter she had been staying at, just down the street.
"We said goodbye, I got maybe four steps towards the house and I heard, 'Get out of the car.'
"I turned around and there were three cop cars - one in the driveway and two in the road. I ran back to Devon, because I knew he was holding a gun, and I tried to get him to give me the gun."
But LaFleur, she said, was defiant.
"He wouldn't put down the gun," she recalled. "They said very clearly at least twice, very loudly, 'Put down the gun. Put down the gun.'

"And his response was to wave the gun over his head, saying 'What are you gonna do?' He was very defiant. His eyes were completely different than I've ever seen. He was very determined," she recalled.
"I tried to take the gun away from his hands, but he pulled the gun behind him... I think he was protecting me."
Knetsch said she believes police gave LaFleur an opportunity to surrender. Within 30 seconds, he had been fatally shot.
"He was waving the gun above him. As soon as he lowered it a bit towards them...," her voice once again trailing off.
"I told them after (the shooting), 'It's not a real gun,' and the police officer said, 'We can't take that chance.'"
Knetsch said LaFleur's family is still coping with the shock of his death.
"Devon was greatly loved, very charismatic," she said. "Everybody loved him. He was an incredibly generous and caring person."
